# Analysis

### Descriptive Analysis

In our data set, as the carat size increases, the price of the diamond
increases. This would be a positive correlation between the carat size
and the diamond's price. There are some fluctuating prices that appear
at certain, specific carat sizes, such as 1.5 carat diamonds. This could
be because of the new popularity of lab-grown diamonds, where there are
an abundance of carats at different prices since the demand might set
different prices depending on the jeweler. This also occurs in this data
set at 2 carats and 3 carats, indicating these carats might be the most
popular for individuals buying the diamonds in this data set. We can
also see that in this data set, it is much less common to see super
large and super expensive carats, and more common to see smaller, less
expensive diamonds. This makes sense since there are fewer "premium" cut
diamonds, which tend to be more expensive.

### Inferential Analysis

I used a wilcoxon rank-sum test because my data set, when plotted as a
histogram, had a strong right skew. I also wanted to compare a
continuous outcome between 2 groups, the price and the color grade of
the diamonds rated "E" and "I", which affirmed my decision to use a
wilcoxon rank-sum test. The p-value for this test was \<2.2e-16. Based
on this p-value, since it is below a significance level of 0.05, this
provides evidence against the null hypothesis and indicates the data is
inconsistent with the null hypothesis. To conclude, I was able to reject
the null hypothesis that the average price of diamonds with a color
value of "E" is the same as diamonds with a color value of "I". I might
be making a type I error because I am rejecting the null hypothesis when
it could actually be true. For example, I could conclude that color
grade "E" and "I" diamonds have an difference in average price when in
reality, they might be the same average price, which would support the
null hypothesis instead of reject it.

### Regression Analysis

My model had the outcome as price and the predictors as carat and
diamond cut. Key results showed that the direction of all of the
predictor coefficients was positive, indicating an increase in price
when there was an increase in carat size as well as when the quality of
the diamond cut increased on the diamond cut scale compared to the
"fair" cut diamond. All of the predictor coefficients had statistical
significance, which implies that the price does variably change when you
go up on the scale of diamond quality. A diamond that could be
considered more "rare" or harder to obtain, such as a large carat
diamond or an "ideal" cut of diamond, will be more expensive than a
"fair" cut diamond or a lower carat size. Some concerns when running the
diagnostic checks was the residual deviation away from zero as the
fitted values increased in the residuals vs. fitted plot. This indicates
that the residuals might not be normally distributed, and that would
mean that the linear regression might not be an appropriate regression
analysis for this, since a necessity of linear regression is that the
residuals are normally distributed. I am not as concerned about the QQ
plot, since the values tend to stay on the plot line and only deviate
away on the tail ends, so this makes me feel less concerned about the
concerns I had with the residual vs. fitted plot. Overall, I think the
data passed the diagnostic checks and the regression analysis was
successfully run.
